interviewQuestions.question: How does Garbage Collection work in Java? Describe the Generational Hypothesis.
interviewQuestions.answer: Most allocated objects die young. Java divides heap into Young Generation (Eden + Survivor spaces S0, S1) and Old Generation. Minor GC collects short-lived objects from Eden quickly; surviving objects are promoted to Old Generation, where Major/Full GC occurs less frequently.
interviewQuestions.tips: Mention Eden, Survivor spaces, and tenure threshold.

interviewQuestions.question: What is the contract between equals() and hashCode()?
interviewQuestions.answer: 1. If two objects are equal according to equals(), they must produce the same hashCode(). 2. If two objects have the same hashCode(), they are not necessarily equal (hash collision).
interviewQuestions.tips: Highlight that violating rule 1 breaks HashMaps.

examQuestions.question: Explain Java Memory Model including Stack, Heap, and Metaspace.
examQuestions.solutionGuide: Stack stores primitive local variables and method frames; Heap stores objects; Metaspace stores class metadata and static variables.

practiceExercises: Implement a LRU Cache in Java using LinkedHashMap.
revisionNotes: equals() and hashCode() must be overridden together
Young Gen: Eden + S0 + S1; Old Gen holds long-lived objects

topics.title: Complexity Analysis and Big-O Notation
topics.summary: Asymptotic notation (Big-O, Big-Omega, Big-Theta), worst-case, best-case, average-case, and amortized complexity.
topics.definition: Big-O notation is a mathematical notation that describes the limiting behavior of a function when the argument tends towards a particular value or infinity, classifying algorithms according to their running time or space requirements.
topics.detailedExplanation: Asymptotic analysis evaluates how algorithm performance scales as input size n approaches infinity, independent of machine architecture. Big-O represents the asymptotic upper bound (worst-case growth rate), Big-Omega (Ω) represents the lower bound (best-case), and Big-Theta (Θ) represents a tight bound where upper and lower bounds match. Common complexity classes in order: O(1) constant < O(log n) logarithmic < O(n) linear < O(n log n) linearithmic < O(n^2) quadratic < O(2^n) exponential < O(n!) factorial.
typesAndClassifications: Space Complexity (Auxiliary space vs Total space)
Average vs Worst vs Best case
importantConcepts: Amortized analysis (e.g. ArrayList doubling is amortized O(1))
practicalApplications: Selecting optimal algorithms for production scalability
Code profiling and performance bottleneck analysis

codeExamples.title: ComplexityExamples.java
codeExamples.explanation: Halving search space at each iteration achieves O(log n) complexity.

complexityAnalysis.timeComplexity: Comparison table: O(1) to O(n!)
complexityAnalysis.explanation: Classifies algorithm efficiency.

commonMistakes: Assuming recursive algorithms with no loops are automatically O(1)
Ignoring auxiliary stack space in recursion when calculating space complexity

interviewQuestions.question: What is Amortized Time Complexity? Give an example.
interviewQuestions.answer: Amortized time is the average time taken per operation over a sequence of operations. For example, inserting into a dynamic array (ArrayList) is usually O(1), but occasionally triggers an O(n) array resizing. Spread across n insertions, the average cost per insertion is amortized O(1).
interviewQuestions.tips: Use dynamic array resizing as the canonical illustration.

examQuestions.question: Define Big-O, Big-Omega, and Big-Theta notations with formal mathematical definitions and graphs.
examQuestions.solutionGuide: Write definitions: f(n) <= c*g(n) for n >= n0; draw growth curve charts.

practiceExercises: Find the time and space complexity of computing the n-th Fibonacci number recursively vs iteratively.
revisionNotes: Big-O = Upper bound; Big-Omega = Lower bound; Big-Theta = Tight bound
Growth: O(1) < O(log n) < O(n) < O(n log n) < O(n^2) < O(2^n) < O(n!)

topics.title: Arrays and Strings in DSA
topics.summary: Contiguous memory, 2-pointer technique, sliding window, prefix sums, and Kadane's algorithm.
topics.definition: An array is a data structure consisting of a collection of elements identified by index, stored in contiguous memory locations.
topics.detailedExplanation: Contiguous memory allocation allows O(1) random access via index arithmetic: address = base_address + index * element_size. Key algorithmic patterns on arrays include: Two-Pointer Technique (converging from opposite ends or fast/slow pointer), Sliding Window (tracking subarray metrics in O(n) instead of O(n^2)), Prefix Sum Arrays (answering range sum queries in O(1) after O(n) preprocessing), and Kadane's algorithm for maximum subarray sum in O(n).
importantConcepts: Sliding Window Pattern (Fixed and Variable size)

codeExamples.title: KadanesAlgorithm.java
codeExamples.explanation: Calculates maximum subarray sum in single pass O(n) time and O(1) space.

complexityAnalysis.timeComplexity: O(n) time
complexityAnalysis.explanation: Optimal single pass traversal.

commonMistakes: Integer overflow when calculating midpoint: use low + (high - low) / 2 instead of (low + high) / 2

interviewQuestions.question: Explain the Sliding Window technique with an example problem.
interviewQuestions.answer: The sliding window maintains a window over an array/string defined by two pointers (left and right). Instead of recalculating the window properties in O(k), we slide the window by adding the incoming element and subtracting the outgoing element in O(1), reducing overall time from O(n*k) to O(n).
interviewQuestions.tips: Give Maximum Sum Subarray of size K as example.

examQuestions.question: Write an algorithm for Kadane's method to find the maximum sum contiguous subarray.
examQuestions.solutionGuide: Explain local maximum vs global maximum; step-by-step trace on array [-2,1,-3,4,-1,2,1,-5,4].

practiceExercises: Solve the Longest Substring Without Repeating Characters problem using a sliding window and HashSet.
revisionNotes: Two pointers: O(n) time for sorted array search and palindromes
Sliding window: converts nested O(n^2) subarray problems to O(n)
Kadane: max(nums[i], currentMax + nums[i])

topics.title: Linked Lists
topics.summary: Singly linked lists, doubly linked lists, circular lists, pointer reversal, Floyd's cycle detection, and merge sort on lists.
topics.definition: A linked list is a linear data structure where elements (nodes) are stored non-contiguously in memory, with each node containing data and a reference (pointer) to the next node.
topics.detailedExplanation: Unlike arrays, linked lists allow O(1) insertions and deletions at known pointer locations without shifting elements, at the cost of O(n) sequential access. Singly linked lists point forward; doubly linked lists point forward and backward. Key techniques include dummy head nodes to simplify edge cases, in-place pointer reversal, and Floyd's Cycle Detection (Tortoise and Hare algorithm using slow and fast pointers).
importantConcepts: Fast and slow pointer to find midpoint

codeExamples.title: ReverseLinkedList.java
codeExamples.explanation: Reverses pointers in-place in O(n) time and O(1) auxiliary space.

complexityAnalysis.timeComplexity: Search: O(n); Insertion at head: O(1); Deletion at head: O(1)
complexityAnalysis.explanation: Node pointer updates take constant time.

commonMistakes: Losing the reference to the rest of the list when updating next pointers
NullPointerException when accessing fast.next.next without checking fast.next != null

interviewQuestions.question: How does Floyd's Cycle Detection algorithm work and how do you find the start of the cycle?
interviewQuestions.answer: Use slow pointer (1 step) and fast pointer (2 steps). If they meet, a cycle exists. To find the entry node: reset slow to head, keep fast at meeting point, and advance both 1 step at a time; they will meet at the cycle start due to modular distance math (2(F + a) = F + a + nC => F = nC - a).
interviewQuestions.tips: Derive the mathematical proof step.

examQuestions.question: Write an algorithm to reverse a singly linked list iteratively and recursively.
examQuestions.solutionGuide: Present both iterative pointer tracking and recursive stack unwinding approaches.

practiceExercises: Merge two sorted linked lists into one sorted linked list in O(n) time and O(1) extra space.
revisionNotes: Insertion at head: O(1); search: O(n)
Floyd cycle detection: slow (1 step) meets fast (2 steps)
Dummy head prevents null checks on edge insertions

topics.title: Stacks and Queues
topics.summary: LIFO and FIFO principles, array and linked list implementations, Monotonic Stack, Circular Queue, and Deque.
topics.definition: A stack is a LIFO (Last-In-First-Out) linear data structure, while a queue is a FIFO (First-In-First-Out) linear data structure.
topics.detailedExplanation: Stacks support push, pop, and peek in O(1). They power function call stacks, balanced parenthesis checking, and expression evaluation (infix to postfix). Monotonic Stacks maintain elements in strictly increasing or decreasing order, solving Next Greater Element in O(n). Queues support enqueue and dequeue in O(1). Circular Queues utilize modulo arithmetic ((rear + 1) % capacity) to prevent memory waste in fixed arrays. Deques (Double-Ended Queues) allow O(1) operations at both ends.
typesAndClassifications: Queue (Simple Queue, Circular Queue, PriorityQueue, Deque)
importantConcepts: Next Greater Element using Monotonic Stack

codeExamples.title: BalancedParentheses.java
codeExamples.explanation: Uses ArrayDeque as stack to validate balanced brackets in O(n) time.

complexityAnalysis.timeComplexity: Push/Pop/Enqueue/Dequeue: O(1)
complexityAnalysis.explanation: All fundamental operations take constant time.

commonMistakes: Using java.util.Stack (which is synchronized and extends legacy Vector) instead of ArrayDeque

interviewQuestions.question: How do you implement a Queue using two Stacks?
interviewQuestions.answer: Use stackIn for enqueue operations (push to stackIn). For dequeue: if stackOut is empty, transfer all elements from stackIn to stackOut (reversing their order to FIFO); then pop from stackOut. Amortized time per operation is O(1).
interviewQuestions.tips: Emphasize that each element is moved at most twice, giving amortized O(1).

examQuestions.question: Convert the following infix expression to postfix using a stack: (A + B) * (C - D) / E
examQuestions.solutionGuide: Show step-by-step table with scanned symbol, stack state, and postfix expression output.

practiceExercises: Find the Next Greater Element for each element in an array using a monotonic stack.
revisionNotes: Stack = LIFO; Queue = FIFO
Use ArrayDeque instead of legacy Stack
Monotonic stack solves Next Greater Element in O(n)

topics.title: Hashing and Hash Tables
topics.summary: Hash functions, collision resolution (chaining vs open addressing), load factor, rehashing, and two-sum problem.
topics.definition: Hashing is a technique that maps large keys to smaller fixed-size table indices using a mathematical hash function, enabling constant-time average operations.
topics.detailedExplanation: A Hash Table maps keys to values. A good hash function distributes keys uniformly across table slots. When two keys hash to the same index (collision), resolution strategies include Separate Chaining (each bucket points to a linked list or red-black tree) and Open Addressing (Linear Probing, Quadratic Probing, Double Hashing). Load Factor (α = n / m) measures table fullness; when α exceeds a threshold (typically 0.75), the table rehashes by doubling its capacity.
typesAndClassifications: Open Addressing (Linear Probing, Quadratic Probing, Double Hashing)
importantConcepts: Hash function properties: Determinism, Uniformity, Speed

codeExamples.title: TwoSum.java
codeExamples.explanation: Reduces Two-Sum from O(n^2) brute force to O(n) time using HashMap lookup.

complexityAnalysis.timeComplexity: Average: O(1) for insert/search/delete; Worst: O(n)
complexityAnalysis.explanation: Uniform distribution provides average constant time.

commonMistakes: Clustering in linear probing when hash collisions group together into long contiguous runs

interviewQuestions.question: What is the difference between Separate Chaining and Open Addressing?
interviewQuestions.answer: Separate chaining stores collided elements in external data structures (linked lists/trees) at each bucket slot; capacity is unbounded. Open addressing stores all elements inside the table array itself, probing alternate empty slots upon collision; table cannot exceed array capacity without rehashing.
interviewQuestions.tips: Mention cache locality advantages of open addressing vs pointer overhead of chaining.

examQuestions.question: Explain collision resolution techniques in hash tables with suitable diagrams.
examQuestions.solutionGuide: Detail separate chaining, linear probing, quadratic probing, and double hashing formulas.

practiceExercises: Design a custom HashMap with put, get, and remove using separate chaining.
revisionNotes: Average time: O(1); Worst time: O(n)
Separate Chaining: uses linked lists/trees at buckets
Open Addressing: probes for next empty slot inside table

topics.title: Searching and Sorting Algorithms
topics.summary: Binary Search, Quick Sort (partition schemes), Merge Sort, Heap Sort, Counting Sort, stability, and comparison sort lower bound.
topics.definition: Searching algorithms retrieve stored information from data structures, while sorting algorithms rearrange elements into numerical or lexicographical order.
topics.detailedExplanation: Binary Search requires a sorted array, dividing search space in half each step (O(log n)). Comparison sorting algorithms cannot beat O(n log n) in the worst case (proven by decision trees). Merge Sort divides array into halves, recursively sorts, and merges them in O(n log n) time and O(n) space (stable). Quick Sort picks a pivot, partitions elements around the pivot, and recursively sorts; average O(n log n), worst O(n^2) if pivot is poorly chosen. Counting Sort sorts in O(n + k) non-comparison time for bounded integer ranges.
typesAndClassifications: Comparison Sorts (Merge, Quick, Heap, Bubble, Insertion, Selection)
importantConcepts: Lomuto vs Hoare partition schemes in QuickSort
Stability: preserving relative order of equal keys
O(n log n) theoretical lower bound for comparison sorting

codeExamples.title: MergeSort.java
codeExamples.explanation: Guarantees O(n log n) time in all cases with stable element ordering.

complexityAnalysis.timeComplexity: Merge Sort: O(n log n) always; Quick Sort: O(n log n) avg, O(n^2) worst; Counting Sort: O(n + k)
complexityAnalysis.spaceComplexity: Merge Sort: O(n); Quick Sort: O(log n) stack
complexityAnalysis.explanation: Comparison lower bound is Omega(n log n).

commonMistakes: Assuming QuickSort is always faster than MergeSort (QuickSort has poor worst-case if pivot is extremal)

interviewQuestions.question: Why is QuickSort preferred over MergeSort for arrays, but MergeSort preferred for linked lists?
interviewQuestions.answer: For arrays, QuickSort has better cache locality and in-place O(log n) stack space without O(n) auxiliary allocation. For linked lists, elements are non-contiguous anyway, and MergeSort can merge lists in O(1) auxiliary space without extra node copying.
interviewQuestions.tips: Highlight CPU cache locality and in-place partitioning.

examQuestions.question: Prove that any comparison-based sorting algorithm requires at least Omega(n log n) comparisons in the worst case.
examQuestions.solutionGuide: Use decision tree model: n! permutations require tree height h >= log2(n!) = Omega(n log n) by Stirling's approximation.

practiceExercises: Implement QuickSort with random pivot selection and 3-way partitioning for duplicate keys.
revisionNotes: MergeSort: O(n log n) guaranteed, stable, O(n) space
QuickSort: O(n log n) average, unstable, in-place
CountingSort: O(n + k) non-comparison sort

topics.title: Trees and Binary Search Trees (BST)
topics.summary: Tree terminology, traversals (Inorder, Preorder, Postorder, Level Order), BST properties, validation, and LCA.
topics.definition: A tree is a non-linear hierarchical data structure consisting of nodes connected by edges, with a root node and subtrees.
topics.detailedExplanation: A Binary Tree has at most 2 children per node. Binary Search Tree (BST) maintains the invariant: all nodes in the left subtree have keys < root key, and all nodes in the right subtree have keys > root key. Inorder traversal of a BST yields elements in strictly sorted ascending order. Operations (search, insert, delete) run in O(h) time, where h is tree height (O(log n) if balanced, O(n) if skewed). Self-balancing trees (AVL, Red-Black) maintain h = O(log n).
importantConcepts: Inorder, Preorder, Postorder, and Level-order (BFS) traversals
BST search, insertion, and 3-case node deletion (0, 1, or 2 children)

codeExamples.title: ValidateBST.java
codeExamples.explanation: Validates BST using range constraints passed down recursively.

complexityAnalysis.timeComplexity: Traversals: O(n); BST Search/Insert/Delete: O(h) where h is O(log n) balanced or O(n) skewed
complexityAnalysis.explanation: Height governs tree efficiency.

commonMistakes: Validating BST by checking only immediate children instead of the entire subtree range

interviewQuestions.question: How do you delete a node with two children from a Binary Search Tree?
interviewQuestions.answer: Find the node's inorder successor (smallest node in right subtree) or inorder predecessor (largest in left subtree). Copy its value to the target node, then recursively delete that successor node (which has at most one child).
interviewQuestions.tips: Walk through the 3 deletion cases: leaf, 1 child, 2 children.

examQuestions.question: Write algorithms for Inorder, Preorder, and Postorder tree traversals recursively and iteratively.
examQuestions.solutionGuide: Provide code and demonstrate traversal orders on a sample 7-node tree.

practiceExercises: Find the Lowest Common Ancestor (LCA) of two nodes in a Binary Search Tree.
revisionNotes: Inorder traversal of BST gives sorted keys
Balanced BST operations take O(log n); skewed tree degenerates to O(n) linked list

topics.title: Heaps and Priority Queues
topics.summary: Min-Heap and Max-Heap, array representation, heapify algorithm (O(n) build-heap), HeapSort, and Top-K elements.
topics.definition: A binary heap is a complete binary tree that satisfies the heap property: in a max-heap, every parent node is >= its children; in a min-heap, every parent node is <= its children.
topics.detailedExplanation: Because a binary heap is a complete binary tree, it can be compactly stored in an array without pointer overhead. For node at index i: parent is (i - 1) / 2, left child is 2*i + 1, right child is 2*i + 2. Insertion adds element at the end and bubbles up (sift-up) in O(log n). Extracting root moves the last element to root and sifts down in O(log n). Building a heap from an arbitrary array takes O(n) time using bottom-up sift-down (Build-Heap theorem).
importantConcepts: Array index math for binary heap
Build-Heap in O(n) time vs O(n log n) repeated insertions
HeapSort: O(n log n) in-place unstable sort

codeExamples.title: KthLargest.java
codeExamples.explanation: Finds k-th largest element in O(n log k) time using a min-heap of size k.

complexityAnalysis.timeComplexity: Insert/Extract: O(log n); Peek: O(1); Build Heap: O(n)
complexityAnalysis.explanation: Build heap theorem sum converges to O(n).

commonMistakes: Believing Build-Heap takes O(n log n) time (bottom-up sift-down is proven O(n))

interviewQuestions.question: Why does building a binary heap take O(n) time instead of O(n log n)?
interviewQuestions.answer: In bottom-up heap construction, most nodes are near the bottom of the tree where height is small. Summing nodes * height across levels yields sum_{h=0}^{log n} (n / 2^(h+1)) * h = n * sum (h / 2^h), which mathematically converges to 2n = O(n).
interviewQuestions.tips: Explain that leaves (n/2 nodes) require 0 swaps.

examQuestions.question: Explain HeapSort with an example and analyze its time and space complexity.
examQuestions.solutionGuide: 1. Build max heap O(n), 2. Swap root with end and heapify O(n log n); show total O(n log n) time and O(1) space.

practiceExercises: Design a Data Stream Median Finder using a Max-Heap and Min-Heap.
revisionNotes: Complete binary tree stored in contiguous array
Parent: (i-1)/2; Left: 2i+1; Right: 2i+2
Build Heap is O(n); Insert/Delete is O(log n)

topics.title: Graphs, BFS, and DFS
topics.summary: Graph representations (Adjacency List vs Matrix), Breadth-First Search (queue), Depth-First Search (stack/recursion), cycle detection, and topological sort.
topics.definition: A graph is a non-linear data structure consisting of a finite set of vertices (nodes) and edges connecting pairs of vertices.
topics.detailedExplanation: Graphs can be directed or undirected, weighted or unweighted. Representations include Adjacency Matrix (O(V^2) space, O(1) edge lookup) and Adjacency List (O(V + E) space, optimal for sparse graphs). BFS explores neighbor by neighbor using a Queue, finding the shortest path in unweighted graphs. DFS explores deep along each branch using recursion or a Stack, used for cycle detection, topological sorting (Kahn's algorithm or DFS post-order), and connected components.
importantConcepts: Adjacency List vs Adjacency Matrix trade-offs
BFS for shortest path in unweighted graphs
DFS for connectivity, cycle detection, topological sort
Visited array to prevent infinite cycles
practicalApplications: Dependency resolution in package managers (npm, maven via Topological Sort)

codeExamples.title: BfsGraph.java
codeExamples.explanation: Traverses connected graph component level-by-level in O(V + E) time.

complexityAnalysis.timeComplexity: BFS & DFS: O(V + E) with Adjacency List; O(V^2) with Adjacency Matrix
complexityAnalysis.spaceComplexity: O(V) for visited array and queue/call stack
complexityAnalysis.explanation: Each vertex and edge visited once.

commonMistakes: Forgetting to mark a vertex as visited when pushing to queue in BFS, causing duplicate queue entries

interviewQuestions.question: How do you detect a cycle in a directed graph versus an undirected graph?
interviewQuestions.answer: In an undirected graph, DFS detects a cycle if an adjacent visited node is not the parent. In a directed graph, that is insufficient; DFS must track nodes currently in the recursion stack (back-edges) using a 3-state coloring (Unvisited, Visiting, Visited).
interviewQuestions.tips: Highlight back-edges and 3-color states for directed graphs.

examQuestions.question: Explain Topological Sorting of a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) using Kahn's Algorithm (indegree).
examQuestions.solutionGuide: Compute in-degrees, push 0 in-degree nodes to queue, process and decrement neighbor in-degrees.

practiceExercises: Implement Course Schedule problem using Kahn's topological sort to detect cyclic prerequisites.
revisionNotes: Adjacency List takes O(V + E) space; Matrix takes O(V^2)
BFS uses Queue and finds unweighted shortest path
DFS uses Stack/Recursion and detects cycles

topics.title: Greedy Algorithms and Dynamic Programming
topics.summary: Greedy choice property, optimal substructure, overlapping subproblems, memoization vs tabulation, 0/1 Knapsack, and LCS.
topics.definition: Greedy algorithms make the locally optimal choice at each step hoping for a global optimum, while Dynamic Programming solves problems with overlapping subproblems and optimal substructure by caching results.
topics.detailedExplanation: Greedy works when local choices guarantee global optimality (e.g. Fractional Knapsack, Dijkstra, Huffman Coding). When greedy fails, Dynamic Programming (DP) is required. DP solves problems having: 1. Optimal Substructure (optimal solution contains optimal solutions to subproblems) and 2. Overlapping Subproblems (subproblems recur repeatedly). DP approaches include Top-Down with Memoization (recursive + cache) and Bottom-Up with Tabulation (iterative table building). Classic problems: 0/1 Knapsack, Longest Common Subsequence (LCS), Coin Change.
importantConcepts: State representation and transitions in DP
practicalApplications: Text diff comparison tools (LCS / git diff)

codeExamples.title: CoinChangeDP.java
codeExamples.explanation: Computes minimum coins to make amount using bottom-up tabulation in O(amount * coins) time.

complexityAnalysis.timeComplexity: Coin Change: O(amount * n); 0/1 Knapsack: O(n * W)
complexityAnalysis.explanation: Pseudo-polynomial time complexity based on numeric capacity.

commonMistakes: Attempting to apply greedy heuristics to 0/1 Knapsack where dynamic programming is strictly required

interviewQuestions.question: What is the difference between Memoization and Tabulation in Dynamic Programming?
interviewQuestions.answer: Memoization is Top-Down, executing recursively from original problem and caching results on demand. Tabulation is Bottom-Up, iteratively filling a table starting from base cases, avoiding recursion stack overflow and often allowing space optimization.
interviewQuestions.tips: Mention recursion stack overhead vs cache locality.

examQuestions.question: Formulate the 0/1 Knapsack problem and derive its Dynamic Programming recurrence relation with a complete algorithm.
examQuestions.solutionGuide: Recurrence: dp[i][w] = max(dp[i-1][w], val[i-1] + dp[i-1][w-wt[i-1]]); trace on table.

practiceExercises: Solve Longest Common Subsequence (LCS) and reconstruct the common string.
revisionNotes: Greedy: local optimal = global optimal
DP: optimal substructure + overlapping subproblems
Memoization is Top-Down; Tabulation is Bottom-Up

topics.title: Database Fundamentals and Architecture
topics.summary: File system vs DBMS, 3-Schema Architecture, Data Independence, DDL, DML, DCL, and TCL.
topics.definition: A Database Management System (DBMS) is software that manages collections of related data, providing efficient, secure, and reliable data storage, retrieval, and modification.
topics.detailedExplanation: Traditional file systems suffer from data redundancy, inconsistency, difficult concurrent access, and security issues. The ANSI/SPARC 3-Schema Architecture decouples database representation into: 1. External Level (user views), 2. Conceptual Level (logical schema of tables, relations, constraints), and 3. Internal Level (physical storage on disk, indexes, file organization). Logical Data Independence isolates external views from conceptual changes; Physical Data Independence isolates conceptual schema from physical storage modifications.
importantConcepts: SQL command types: DDL, DML, DQL, DCL, TCL

codeExamples.title: DdlDmlCommands.sql
codeExamples.explanation: Shows schema definition (DDL) and record insertion (DML).

complexityAnalysis.timeComplexity: Index lookup O(log n); Full table scan O(n)
complexityAnalysis.explanation: DBMS accesses pages via buffer pool manager.

commonMistakes: Confusing logical schema with physical table file allocation on disk

interviewQuestions.question: What is Data Independence in DBMS and why is it important?
interviewQuestions.answer: Data Independence allows modifying schema definition at one level without altering schema at the next higher level. Logical independence allows altering table structure without modifying application views. Physical independence allows reorganizing disk storage or indexes without altering table definitions.
interviewQuestions.tips: Contrast logical vs physical independence.

examQuestions.question: Explain the 3-tier ANSI/SPARC architecture of DBMS with a neat diagram.
examQuestions.solutionGuide: Draw External, Conceptual, and Internal levels with mappings and explain data independence.

practiceExercises: Design a conceptual schema for a University Course Registration System.
revisionNotes: File systems have redundancy and anomalies; DBMS solves them
3 levels: External, Conceptual, Internal
Physical data independence: modify disk without breaking queries

topics.title: Entity-Relationship (ER) Modeling
topics.summary: Entities, attributes (simple, composite, multivalued, derived), relationships, cardinalities, weak entities, and ER-to-Relational mapping.
topics.definition: Entity-Relationship (ER) modeling is a conceptual data modeling approach that visually describes data entities, their attributes, and relationships in a business domain.
topics.detailedExplanation: An Entity is a distinguishable real-world object. Attributes can be simple, composite (e.g. Name: First, Last), multivalued (e.g. PhoneNumbers), or derived (e.g. Age computed from DOB). Relationships represent associations between entities with cardinality ratios (1:1, 1:N, M:N) and participation constraints (total vs partial). A Weak Entity cannot be identified uniquely by its own attributes alone and depends on an identifying relationship with a strong entity via a partial key (discriminator).
importantConcepts: Weak entity sets and identifying relationships
Converting ER diagrams into relational tables
practicalApplications: System design blueprints for new applications
Database refactoring and enterprise data governance

codeExamples.title: JunctionTable.sql
codeExamples.code:
-- Mapping Many-to-Many (M:N) relationship between Students and Courses
CREATE TABLE student_courses (
    student_id INT REFERENCES students(id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
    course_id INT REFERENCES courses(id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
    enrollment_date DATE DEFAULT CURRENT_DATE,
    PRIMARY KEY (student_id, course_id)
);
codeExamples.explanation: Junction table resolves M:N relationship with composite primary key.

complexityAnalysis.timeComplexity: Join queries on foreign key indexes O(log n)
complexityAnalysis.explanation: Foreign keys index lookups.

commonMistakes: Attempting to store multivalued attributes directly in a single column instead of creating a separate related table

interviewQuestions.question: How is a Weak Entity set converted into relational schema?
interviewQuestions.answer: A weak entity set becomes a table containing all its simple attributes plus the primary key of its identifying strong entity as a foreign key. The primary key of the new table is the combination of the strong entity primary key and the weak entity partial key (discriminator).
interviewQuestions.tips: Mention partial key / discriminator.

examQuestions.question: Draw an ER diagram for a Hospital Management System showing all attributes, relationships, cardinalities, and weak entities.
examQuestions.solutionGuide: Include Patient, Doctor, Department, Appointment, Ward, and Treatment entities.

practiceExercises: Convert an M:N ER diagram with attributes on the relationship into relational tables.
revisionNotes: Rectangles = Entities; Diamonds = Relationships; Ovals = Attributes; Double rectangle = Weak entity
M:N relationship requires an associative/junction table

topics.title: Relational Model, Keys, and Constraints
topics.summary: Tuples, attributes, domains, Candidate Key, Primary Key, Super Key, Foreign Key, and Integrity Constraints.
topics.definition: The Relational Model represents data in relations (tables) consisting of rows (tuples) and columns (attributes), enforcing constraints to maintain integrity.
topics.detailedExplanation: In the relational model, each table represents a relation with unordered unique tuples. A Super Key is any set of attributes that uniquely identifies a tuple. A Candidate Key is a minimal Super Key. One candidate key is chosen as the Primary Key (unique and NOT NULL). An Alternate Key is any unchosen candidate key. A Foreign Key is a set of attributes referencing the primary key of another table, enforcing Referential Integrity (cascading actions: CASCADE, SET NULL, RESTRICT). Domain Constraints enforce valid attribute types.
importantConcepts: Entity Integrity constraint (Primary key cannot be null)
Referential Integrity constraint (Foreign key must match valid primary key or be null)
practicalApplications: Preventing orphaned records in e-commerce orders and customer accounts
Enforcing business rules at the database engine level

codeExamples.title: ConstraintsDemo.sql
codeExamples.code:
CREATE TABLE orders (
    order_id SERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    customer_id INT NOT NULL,
    order_amount NUMERIC(10, 2) CHECK (order_amount > 0),
    order_status VARCHAR(20) DEFAULT 'PENDING',
    CONSTRAINT fk_customer FOREIGN KEY (customer_id) 
        REFERENCES customers(id) ON DELETE RESTRICT
);
codeExamples.explanation: Enforces primary key, check constraint, and referential integrity with ON DELETE RESTRICT.

complexityAnalysis.timeComplexity: Foreign key constraint check on insert O(log n)
complexityAnalysis.explanation: Index lookup on referenced table.

commonMistakes: Deleting parent record when foreign key constraint is set to RESTRICT without deleting dependent child records

interviewQuestions.question: What is the difference between a Super Key and a Candidate Key?
interviewQuestions.answer: A Super Key is any attribute combination that uniquely identifies a tuple, but may contain redundant attributes. A Candidate Key is a minimal super key with no extraneous attributes; removing any attribute destroys uniqueness.
interviewQuestions.tips: Give Candidate Key as minimal Super Key.

examQuestions.question: Explain Entity Integrity and Referential Integrity constraints with examples.
examQuestions.solutionGuide: Define Entity Integrity (PK not null and unique) and Referential Integrity (FK validity, ON DELETE rules).

practiceExercises: Write SQL DDL demonstrating PRIMARY KEY, FOREIGN KEY with ON DELETE CASCADE, and CHECK constraints.
revisionNotes: Candidate Key = Minimal Super Key
Entity Integrity: Primary Key cannot be NULL
Referential Integrity: Foreign Key must reference valid existing record or NULL

topics.title: SQL: Queries, Joins, and Subqueries
topics.summary: SELECT, WHERE, GROUP BY, HAVING, ORDER BY, INNER JOIN, LEFT/RIGHT/FULL OUTER JOIN, correlated subqueries, and window functions.
topics.definition: SQL (Structured Query Language) is the standard declarative language used to query, manipulate, and define data in relational databases.
topics.detailedExplanation: SQL statements execute in a specific logical order: FROM & JOIN -> WHERE -> GROUP BY -> HAVING -> SELECT -> DISTINCT -> ORDER BY -> LIMIT. Joins combine rows from multiple tables based on related columns: INNER JOIN (only matching rows), LEFT OUTER JOIN (all left rows + matching right rows), RIGHT OUTER JOIN, and FULL OUTER JOIN. Subqueries can be scalar, multi-row (IN, ANY, ALL), or Correlated (inner query references outer query row-by-row). Window functions (ROW_NUMBER, RANK, DENSE_RANK, OVER (PARTITION BY ...)) compute calculations across row partitions without collapsing rows like GROUP BY.
importantConcepts: WHERE (filters rows before aggregation) vs HAVING (filters aggregated groups)
Window functions: ROW_NUMBER(), DENSE_RANK(), SUM() OVER()
practicalApplications: User order aggregation and rank computation
ETL pipelines and business intelligence dashboards

codeExamples.title: JoinsAndWindow.sql
codeExamples.code:
-- Top earning employee per department using Window Function
WITH RankedEmployees AS (
    SELECT 
        e.name, 
        d.department_name, 
        e.salary,
        DENSE_RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY e.dept_id ORDER BY e.salary DESC) as rank
    FROM employees e
    INNER JOIN departments d ON e.dept_id = d.id
)
SELECT name, department_name, salary
FROM RankedEmployees
WHERE rank = 1;
codeExamples.explanation: Uses INNER JOIN and DENSE_RANK window function partitioned by department.

complexityAnalysis.timeComplexity: Hash Join: O(M + N); Nested Loop Join: O(M * N) without index; Window function: O(N log N)
complexityAnalysis.explanation: Query planner selects optimal join algorithm.

commonMistakes: Using WHERE to filter aggregated functions instead of HAVING
Accidental Cartesian product when join condition is omitted

interviewQuestions.question: What is the difference between RANK() and DENSE_RANK() window functions in SQL?
interviewQuestions.answer: Both assign ranks based on ordered values. When there are ties, RANK() skips subsequent ranks (e.g., 1, 2, 2, 4), while DENSE_RANK() does not skip rank values (e.g., 1, 2, 2, 3).
interviewQuestions.tips: Provide the sequence 1, 2, 2, 4 vs 1, 2, 2, 3.

examQuestions.question: Explain all types of SQL Joins with syntax, Venn diagrams, and example queries.
examQuestions.solutionGuide: Detail Inner, Left Outer, Right Outer, Full Outer, and Self Join.

practiceExercises: Write a query to find the second highest salary without using LIMIT or TOP keywords.
revisionNotes: Execution order: FROM -> WHERE -> GROUP BY -> HAVING -> SELECT -> ORDER BY
WHERE filters rows; HAVING filters aggregated groups
DENSE_RANK does not skip numbers after ties

topics.title: Normalization and Functional Dependencies
topics.summary: Anomalies (insert, update, delete), Functional Dependencies, Armstrong's Axioms, 1NF, 2NF, 3NF, and BCNF.
topics.definition: Normalization is the systematic process of organizing relational database tables to minimize data redundancy and eliminate insertion, update, and deletion anomalies.
topics.detailedExplanation: Unnormalized tables cause: 1. Insertion Anomaly (cannot insert attribute without unrelated data), 2. Deletion Anomaly (deleting one fact accidentally deletes unrelated facts), and 3. Update Anomaly (modifying data requires updating multiple duplicate rows). Functional Dependency (X -> Y) means X uniquely determines Y. Normal forms progression: 1NF (atomic values, no repeating groups), 2NF (in 1NF and no partial dependencies on candidate key), 3NF (in 2NF and no transitive dependencies; every non-prime attribute is non-transitively dependent on candidate keys), BCNF (Boyce-Codd Normal Form: for every functional dependency X -> Y, X must be a super key).
importantConcepts: Functional Dependencies and Attribute Closure calculation
Lossless Join Decomposition and Dependency Preservation
practicalApplications: Eliminating data corruption in enterprise financial systems

codeExamples.title: Decomposition.txt
codeExamples.code:
Given Table: Enrollment(StudentID, CourseID, Instructor, Office)
FDs: 
  {StudentID, CourseID} -> {Instructor, Office}
  Instructor -> Office (Transitive Dependency on non-candidate key)

Decomposition to 3NF/BCNF:
Table 1: CourseInstructor(CourseID, Instructor, Office) with Instructor -> Office
Table 2: StudentEnrollment(StudentID, CourseID)
Eliminates redundancy and update anomalies.
codeExamples.explanation: Decomposes transitive dependency into separate relation.

complexityAnalysis.timeComplexity: Attribute closure computation O(n * |FD|)
complexityAnalysis.explanation: Saves disk space and avoids redundant writes.

commonMistakes: Decomposing tables without verifying Lossless Join decomposition property (R1 ∩ R2 -> R1 or R1 ∩ R2 -> R2)

interviewQuestions.question: What is the difference between 3NF and BCNF?
interviewQuestions.answer: In 3NF, for every functional dependency X -> Y, either X is a super key OR Y is a prime attribute (part of any candidate key). BCNF is stricter: X MUST be a super key for every dependency X -> Y, with no exception for prime attributes.
interviewQuestions.tips: Highlight the "Y is a prime attribute" relaxation in 3NF.

examQuestions.question: Given a relation R(A, B, C, D, E) and FDs {A -> BC, CD -> E, B -> D, E -> A}. Find the candidate keys and determine the highest normal form.
examQuestions.solutionGuide: Compute attribute closures for A+, B+, etc. Determine candidate keys {A}, {E}, {CD}, {BC}. Check B -> D violations to classify NF.

practiceExercises: Check whether decomposition of R(A, B, C, D) with FDs into R1(A, B) and R2(B, C, D) is lossless.
revisionNotes: 1NF = Atomic values only
2NF = No partial dependency (non-prime dependent on subset of composite key)
3NF = No transitive dependency
BCNF = For X -> Y, X must be a Super Key

topics.title: Transactions and ACID Properties
topics.summary: Transaction states, Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability, write-ahead logging (WAL), and commit/rollback.
topics.definition: A database transaction is a logical unit of work comprising one or more database operations that must execute with complete integrity.
topics.detailedExplanation: Transactions adhere to the ACID properties: Atomicity (all operations succeed or all roll back; "all or nothing", implemented via Write-Ahead Logging/undo logs), Consistency (database transitions from one valid state satisfying all schema constraints to another), Isolation (concurrent transactions execute without interfering with one another, preventing dirty reads and non-repeatable reads), Durability (once committed, changes persist permanently even after hardware crashes or power failures, via redo logs / WAL). Transaction states include: Active, Partially Committed, Committed, Failed, and Aborted.
typesAndClassifications: Transaction States (Active, Partially Committed, Committed, Failed, Aborted)
importantConcepts: Write-Ahead Logging (WAL) protocol: log records written to disk before dirty data pages
practicalApplications: Bank fund transfers (deduct from sender and add to receiver atomically)

codeExamples.title: TransactionBlock.sql
codeExamples.explanation: Atomic bank transfer: both accounts update together or both roll back.

complexityAnalysis.timeComplexity: Commit O(1) sequential log append to disk
complexityAnalysis.explanation: Sequential disk write to log is fast.

commonMistakes: Assuming committed transactions can be lost upon sudden power loss (Durability guarantees persistence via WAL flush)

interviewQuestions.question: How does a database engine implement Atomicity and Durability?
interviewQuestions.answer: Via Write-Ahead Logging (WAL). To ensure Atomicity, the Undo Log tracks original values of modified data; if a transaction aborts, undo logs revert dirty writes. To ensure Durability, the Redo Log is flushed to non-volatile disk before acknowledging commit; on crash recovery, unwritten dirty buffer pages are redone from the log.
interviewQuestions.tips: Mention Undo Log for Atomicity and Redo Log for Durability.

examQuestions.question: Explain ACID properties in detail. How does DBMS maintain consistency and durability?
examQuestions.solutionGuide: Define A, C, I, D. Detail shadow paging / WAL for Atomicity and Redo logging for Durability.

practiceExercises: Write a simulated banking transaction in SQL with savepoints and error rollback.
revisionNotes: Atomicity = All or Nothing (Undo log)
Consistency = Invariants preserved
Isolation = No interference (Concurrency control)
Durability = Changes survive crashes (Redo log / WAL)

topics.title: Concurrency Control and Indexing
topics.summary: Schedules (serial, conflict serializable), Two-Phase Locking (2PL), deadlock prevention, B-Tree and B+ Tree indexing, and query execution plans.
topics.definition: Concurrency control coordinates simultaneous transaction execution without conflicts, while indexing creates auxiliary data structures to accelerate data retrieval.
topics.detailedExplanation: Concurrency anomalies include: Dirty Read (reading uncommitted data), Non-repeatable Read (rereading row sees different values), and Phantom Read (rereading range sees newly inserted rows). Conflict Serializability checks if a schedule is equivalent to a serial schedule by building a Precedence Graph (cycle indicates non-serializable). Two-Phase Locking (2PL: Growing Phase where locks are acquired, Shrinking Phase where locks are released) guarantees conflict serializability; Strict 2PL holds exclusive locks until commit. Indexing uses B+ Trees where all data records reside in leaf nodes linked sequentially, enabling both O(log n) point lookups and high-speed range scans.
typesAndClassifications: Isolation Levels (Read Uncommitted, Read Committed, Repeatable Read, Serializable)
Locking Protocols (Shared vs Exclusive locks, 2PL, Strict 2PL)
Indexes (Primary/Clustered, Secondary/Non-clustered, B+ Tree, Hash Index)
importantConcepts: Two-Phase Locking (2PL) Growing and Shrinking phases
B+ Tree structure: Balanced search tree with linked leaf nodes
Clustered index (determines physical row order) vs Non-clustered index
practicalApplications: High-throughput transaction processing in payment gateways
Speeding up SQL queries from minutes to milliseconds via targeted composite indexing

codeExamples.title: IndexCreation.sql
codeExamples.code:
-- Composite Index for multi-column query acceleration
CREATE INDEX idx_orders_customer_date 
ON orders (customer_id, order_date DESC);
-- Analyze query plan
EXPLAIN ANALYZE 
SELECT * FROM orders 
WHERE customer_id = 42 
ORDER BY order_date DESC;
codeExamples.explanation: Uses composite index to satisfy both filter and sorting without file sort.

complexityAnalysis.timeComplexity: B+ Tree Search/Insert/Delete: O(log_B N) where B is fanout (~100-500)
complexityAnalysis.explanation: Shallow tree depth (3-4 levels) minimizes disk I/O.

commonMistakes: Over-indexing tables, which significantly degrades INSERT, UPDATE, and DELETE performance due to index maintenance

interviewQuestions.question: Why are B+ Trees preferred over Binary Search Trees or B-Trees for database indexing?
interviewQuestions.answer: 1. Higher fanout (branching factor) means shallow tree depth (3-4 levels for millions of rows), drastically minimizing disk block I/O. 2. Data records are exclusively stored in leaf nodes, leaving internal nodes purely for routing keys. 3. Leaf nodes are linked as a doubly-linked list, enabling efficient sequential range scans.
interviewQuestions.tips: Highlight high fanout minimizing disk I/O and linked leaves for range queries.

examQuestions.question: What is Conflict Serializability? Test whether schedule S is conflict serializable: r1(x), r2(x), w1(x), r1(y), w2(x), c1, c2.
examQuestions.solutionGuide: Draw Precedence Graph with edges for conflicting read/write pairs. Check for cycles.

practiceExercises: Trace insertion of keys into a B+ Tree with order M=4 and show node splits.
revisionNotes: Strict 2PL prevents cascading rollbacks
B+ Trees have high fanout and linked leaf nodes for range scans
Clustered index physically sorts rows; only 1 per table

topics.title: Operating System Fundamentals and System Calls
topics.summary: Kernel vs User space, dual-mode operation, Interrupts, System Call interface, and monolithic vs microkernel architecture.
topics.definition: An Operating System is system software that acts as an intermediary between computer hardware and the user, managing hardware resources and providing a platform for application execution.
topics.detailedExplanation: Modern CPUs implement Dual-Mode Operation: User Mode (restricted privileges) and Kernel Mode (ring 0, full hardware access). Applications transition from user space to kernel space via System Calls (e.g., read, write, fork, exec) triggered by software interrupts or CPU instructions (sysenter/syscall). The interrupt vector table dispatches system call handlers. Monolithic kernels (Linux) execute all core services in kernel space for maximum performance; Microkernels (Mach, seL4) keep only minimal IPC and memory management in kernel space, running file systems and device drivers as user-space servers for enhanced fault tolerance.
importantConcepts: Dual-mode CPU operation (Ring 3 user vs Ring 0 kernel)

codeExamples.title: ForkSystemCall.c
codeExamples.explanation: fork() duplicates caller process; child receives return value 0, parent receives child PID.

complexityAnalysis.timeComplexity: System call overhead ~100-300 nanoseconds
complexityAnalysis.explanation: Hardware mode switch and register saving overhead.

commonMistakes: Confusing mode switch (switching user to kernel mode for same process) with context switch (saving process state and loading another process)

interviewQuestions.question: What happens during a System Call at the CPU hardware level?
interviewQuestions.answer: The user program executes a syscall/trap instruction, causing the CPU to switch from user mode to kernel mode. Hardware saves program counter and registers onto the kernel stack, consults the Interrupt Descriptor Table (IDT), executes the kernel handler, places results in return registers, and returns to user space via sysret/iret.
interviewQuestions.tips: Mention privilege level change and register saving.

examQuestions.question: Explain Monolithic vs Microkernel architectures with advantages and disadvantages.
examQuestions.solutionGuide: Tabulate performance, crash safety, modularity, and IPC overhead.

practiceExercises: Trace system calls executed by a simple command using strace in Linux.
revisionNotes: Dual-mode: User mode (safe) vs Kernel mode (privileged)
fork() creates child process; exec() replaces address space
Monolithic is faster; Microkernel is more secure/modular

topics.title: Processes, Threads, and CPU Scheduling
topics.summary: PCB, Process states, context switching, FCFS, SJF, SRTF, Round Robin, Priority, and Multilevel Feedback Queue.
topics.definition: A process is an active program in execution containing program code and current activity, while a thread is the smallest schedulable unit of CPU execution within a process.
topics.detailedExplanation: A process address space contains Text, Data, Heap (dynamic memory), and Stack (local variables, return pointers). The Process Control Block (PCB) stores PID, state, PC, CPU registers, memory limits, and open file descriptors. Process states include New, Ready, Running, Waiting, and Terminated. Threads in the same process share code, data, and heap, but have independent stacks and registers. CPU Scheduling algorithms optimize CPU utilization, throughput, turnaround time, waiting time, and response time: FCFS (non-preemptive, convoy effect), SJF/SRTF (provably optimal average waiting time), Round Robin (time quantum slicing), Priority scheduling, and Multilevel Feedback Queue (MLFQ).
typesAndClassifications: Scheduling Algorithms (FCFS, SJF, Round Robin, MLFQ)
importantConcepts: Context Switch latency and cache invalidation
Round Robin time quantum trade-off (too small = excessive context switching; too large = FCFS)
practicalApplications: Multi-core CPU task allocation in Linux CFS (Completely Fair Scheduler)

codeExamples.title: RoundRobinGantt.txt
codeExamples.code:
Processes: P1 (Burst 24ms), P2 (Burst 3ms), P3 (Burst 3ms)
Time Quantum = 4ms

Gantt Chart:
[ P1: 0-4 | P2: 4-7 | P3: 7-10 | P1: 10-14 | P1: 14-18 | P1: 18-22 | P1: 22-26 | P1: 26-30 ]

P2 waiting time: 4 - 0 = 4ms
P3 waiting time: 7 - 0 = 7ms
P1 waiting time: (0) + (10 - 4) = 6ms
Average Waiting Time = (6 + 4 + 7) / 3 = 5.67ms
codeExamples.explanation: Demonstrates Round Robin time slicing preventing starvation.

complexityAnalysis.timeComplexity: Scheduling decision: O(1) in Linux CFS using red-black tree leftmost lookup
complexityAnalysis.spaceComplexity: O(number of processes) for PCB table
complexityAnalysis.explanation: Runqueue maintenance complexity.

commonMistakes: Confusing turnaround time (Completion Time - Arrival Time) with waiting time (Turnaround Time - Burst Time)

interviewQuestions.question: What is the Convoy Effect in CPU scheduling?
interviewQuestions.answer: The convoy effect occurs in non-preemptive scheduling (like FCFS) when a CPU-bound process with a huge burst time occupies the CPU, forcing numerous I/O-bound processes with short bursts to wait in the ready queue, severely degrading CPU and device utilization.
interviewQuestions.tips: Explain how Round Robin or SRTF mitigates the convoy effect.

examQuestions.question: Calculate Average Turnaround Time and Average Waiting Time for processes using Round Robin (Quantum = 2) and Preemptive SJF.
examQuestions.solutionGuide: Draw Gantt charts for both algorithms and tabulate Completion, Turnaround, and Waiting times.

practiceExercises: Simulate FCFS, SJF, and Round Robin algorithms in Java or C.
revisionNotes: Turnaround Time = Completion - Arrival
Waiting Time = Turnaround - Burst
SJF gives minimum average waiting time
Round Robin prevents starvation via time quantum

topics.title: Process Synchronization and Deadlocks
topics.summary: Critical section problem, Peterson's solution, Mutex, Semaphores (binary/counting), Classical problems (Dining Philosophers, Readers-Writers), and Banker's algorithm.
topics.definition: Process synchronization coordinates the execution of concurrent processes that share memory or resources to maintain data consistency.
topics.detailedExplanation: The Critical Section problem requires satisfying three criteria: 1. Mutual Exclusion, 2. Progress, and 3. Bounded Waiting. Synchronization primitives include Mutexes (binary lock with ownership) and Semaphores (integer counters accessed via atomic wait/P and signal/V operations). Classical synchronization problems include Producer-Consumer (bounded buffer), Readers-Writers (starvation trade-offs), and Dining Philosophers. Deadlock occurs when processes are permanently blocked waiting for resources held by each other. Four Coffman conditions for deadlock: Mutual Exclusion, Hold and Wait, No Preemption, and Circular Wait. Banker's Algorithm safely evaluates resource allocation requests to ensure the system remains in a safe state.
typesAndClassifications: Deadlock Handling: Prevention, Avoidance (Banker's), Detection & Recovery, Ignorance (Ostrich)
importantConcepts: 3 Critical Section requirements (Mutual Exclusion, Progress, Bounded Waiting)
Race conditions and atomic operations (Test-And-Set, Compare-And-Swap)
Banker's Algorithm Safe State matrix calculations

codeExamples.title: ProducerConsumerSemaphore.java
codeExamples.explanation: Coordinates producer and consumer using counting and binary semaphores.

complexityAnalysis.timeComplexity: Banker's algorithm: O(m * n^2) where n is processes and m is resource types
complexityAnalysis.spaceComplexity: O(n * m) for Allocation and Need matrices
complexityAnalysis.explanation: Safety algorithm verification complexity.

commonMistakes: Reversing the order of wait/acquire operations in nested semaphores, causing immediate deadlock

interviewQuestions.question: What is the difference between a Mutex and a Semaphore?
interviewQuestions.answer: A Mutex is a locking mechanism with ownership: only the thread that acquired the mutex can release it. A Semaphore is a signaling mechanism with a counter; any thread can signal/release a semaphore. A mutex can be seen as a binary semaphore with ownership semantics.
interviewQuestions.tips: Emphasize ownership and signaling differences.

examQuestions.question: Explain Banker's Algorithm for Deadlock Avoidance. Given Allocation, Max, and Available matrices, determine if the system is in a safe state.
examQuestions.solutionGuide: Compute Need = Max - Allocation. Trace Work and Finish vectors to find safe execution sequence.

practiceExercises: Implement a solution to the Dining Philosophers problem avoiding deadlock using asymmetric seating or semaphores.
revisionNotes: Critical section: Mutual Exclusion, Progress, Bounded Waiting
Coffman conditions: Mutual Exclusion, Hold & Wait, No Preemption, Circular Wait
Banker algorithm ensures system stays in a Safe State

topics.title: Memory Management and Virtual Memory
topics.summary: Paging, Segmentation, TLB, Page Tables, Page Faults, Virtual Memory, and Page Replacement algorithms (FIFO, LRU, Optimal).
topics.definition: Memory management coordinates computer memory, allocating portions to programs, while Virtual Memory provides the illusion of a large contiguous memory space beyond physical RAM.
topics.detailedExplanation: Logical addresses generated by the CPU are mapped to physical memory addresses via the Memory Management Unit (MMU). Paging divides logical address space into fixed-size Pages and physical RAM into Frames of equal size, completely eliminating External Fragmentation (though internal fragmentation remains in the last page). The Translation Lookaside Buffer (TLB) is an associative hardware cache for page table entries. In Virtual Memory, Demanding Paging loads pages only when needed; accessing an unmapped page triggers a Page Fault interrupt. Page replacement algorithms replace an in-RAM page when frames are exhausted: FIFO (suffers from Belady's Anomaly), Optimal (replaces page not used for longest future time; benchmark only), and LRU (Least Recently Used; optimal practical approximation).
typesAndClassifications: Single-level vs Hierarchical / Inverted Page Tables
Page Replacement (FIFO, LRU, Optimal, Clock algorithm)
importantConcepts: Page Table Base Register (PTBR) and TLB hit ratio
Thrashing: excessive paging activity causing CPU utilization to collapse
practicalApplications: Isolated sandbox memory address spaces per process

codeExamples.title: LruPageReplacement.txt
codeExamples.code:
Reference String: 7, 0, 1, 2, 0, 3, 0, 4, 2, 3
Frames: 3

Ref: 7 -> [7, -, -] Page Fault (1)
Ref: 0 -> [7, 0, -] Page Fault (2)
Ref: 1 -> [7, 0, 1] Page Fault (3)
Ref: 2 -> [2, 0, 1] Page Fault (4) (Replaces 7, least recently used)
Ref: 0 -> [2, 0, 1] Hit (0 refreshed)
Ref: 3 -> [2, 0, 3] Page Fault (5) (Replaces 1)
Ref: 0 -> [2, 0, 3] Hit
Ref: 4 -> [4, 0, 3] Page Fault (6) (Replaces 2)
Ref: 2 -> [4, 0, 2] Page Fault (7) (Replaces 3)
Ref: 3 -> [3, 0, 2] Page Fault (8) (Replaces 4)

Total Page Faults = 8
codeExamples.explanation: Traces LRU page replacement with 3 frames.

complexityAnalysis.timeComplexity: Effective Access Time: EAT = hit_ratio * (TLB + RAM) + (1 - hit_ratio) * (TLB + 2*RAM)
complexityAnalysis.spaceComplexity: Page table overhead ~4MB to few GBs
complexityAnalysis.explanation: Multi-level paging saves unused table space.

commonMistakes: Confusing Internal Fragmentation (wasted space inside an allocated fixed-size block/page) with External Fragmentation (free memory broken into scattered unusable small holes)

interviewQuestions.question: What is Thrashing in Virtual Memory and how can the OS resolve it?
interviewQuestions.answer: Thrashing occurs when a computer's virtual memory subsystem is in a constant state of paging, spending more time swapping pages in and out of disk than executing instructions, collapsing CPU utilization. The OS resolves thrashing using the Working Set Model or Page Fault Frequency (PFF) algorithm, swapping out low-priority processes to free memory frames.
interviewQuestions.tips: Mention Working Set Model and Page Fault Frequency.

examQuestions.question: Calculate Effective Memory Access Time (EMAT) if TLB access is 20ns, RAM access is 100ns, and TLB hit ratio is 90%.

practiceExercises: Trace FIFO page replacement on reference string 1, 2, 3, 4, 1, 2, 5, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 for 3 and 4 frames to demonstrate Belady's Anomaly.
revisionNotes: Paging eliminates external fragmentation; pages mapped to frames
TLB is fast hardware cache for page translations
LRU is practical approximation of Optimal algorithm
Belady's Anomaly: FIFO page faults increase when frames increase

topics.title: Network Models: OSI vs TCP/IP
topics.summary: 7 layers of OSI, 4 layers of TCP/IP, encapsulation and decapsulation, PDUs, and device mappings.
topics.definition: Network models provide standardized architectural frameworks that describe how hardware and protocols interoperate to transmit data across interconnected networks.
topics.detailedExplanation: The OSI (Open Systems Interconnection) reference model defines 7 theoretical layers: Physical (bits, cables, hubs), Data Link (frames, MAC addresses, switches), Network (packets, IP addresses, routers), Transport (segments, port numbers, TCP/UDP), Session (dialog control), Presentation (data formatting, encryption, compression), and Application (HTTP, SMTP, FTP). The practical TCP/IP model condenses these into 4 functional layers: Network Access / Link Layer, Internet Layer, Transport Layer, and Application Layer. Data encapsulation wraps protocol headers (PDU) at each layer on transmission, and decapsulation strips headers upon reception.
typesAndClassifications: Packet Data Units: Bits -> Frames -> Packets -> Segments -> Data
importantConcepts: Network devices: Hubs (L1), Switches (L2), Routers (L3), Gateways (L7)
practicalApplications: Designing protocol stacks and microservice networking

codeExamples.title: PduEncapsulation.txt
codeExamples.code:
Layer 7-5 (Application): Data (e.g., HTTP GET / HTTP/1.1)
           ↓ Encapsulate with TCP Header (Source/Dest Port)
Layer 4 (Transport): Segment [ TCP Header | Data ]
           ↓ Encapsulate with IP Header (Source/Dest IP)
Layer 3 (Network): Packet [ IP Header | TCP Header | Data ]
           ↓ Encapsulate with Ethernet Frame Header & FCS Trailer (MACs)
Layer 2 (Data Link): Frame [ Eth Header | IP Header | TCP Header | Data | CRC ]
           ↓ Modulate into raw bits/voltages
Layer 1 (Physical): Bits [ 101011001011... ]
codeExamples.explanation: Visualizes PDU transformation down the protocol stack.

complexityAnalysis.timeComplexity: Header encapsulation O(1) buffer prepending
complexityAnalysis.explanation: Hardware NIC handles link layer framing.

commonMistakes: Assuming switches inspect IP packets (standard Layer 2 switches only inspect MAC addresses)

interviewQuestions.question: What is the difference between the OSI Model and TCP/IP Model?
interviewQuestions.answer: The OSI model is a 7-layer theoretical conceptual model developed by ISO that strictly separates services, interfaces, and protocols. The TCP/IP model is a 4-layer practical protocol suite developed by DoD that powers the global Internet, combining OSI layers 5-7 into the Application layer and layers 1-2 into the Network Access layer.
interviewQuestions.tips: Contrast theoretical OSI vs implemented TCP/IP.

examQuestions.question: Explain the functions of all 7 layers of the OSI reference model with example protocols for each layer.
examQuestions.solutionGuide: Detail Physical, Data Link, Network, Transport, Session, Presentation, Application with protocols.

practiceExercises: Capture network packets using Wireshark and inspect Ethernet, IP, TCP, and HTTP headers.
revisionNotes: PDU: Bits (L1) -> Frames (L2) -> Packets (L3) -> Segments (L4) -> Data (L5-7)
L2 uses MAC addresses; L3 uses IP addresses; L4 uses Port numbers

topics.title: IP Addressing, Subnetting, and Routing
topics.summary: IPv4 vs IPv6, CIDR notation, subnet masks, network and broadcast addresses, VLSM, and routing algorithms (Dijkstra, Distance Vector).
topics.definition: IP addressing assigns unique logical numerical identifiers to devices on a network, while subnetting divides a large network into smaller, efficient subnetworks.
topics.detailedExplanation: IPv4 addresses are 32-bit dotted-decimal numbers (e.g. 192.168.1.1). Classless Inter-Domain Routing (CIDR) uses slash notation (e.g. /24) where the prefix denotes the network bits and the remainder denotes host bits. Subnetting calculates Network ID (bitwise AND of IP and Subnet Mask), First Usable Host, Last Usable Host, and Broadcast Address (host bits set to 1). Total usable hosts = 2^(host_bits) - 2. Routing algorithms determine optimal paths for packets: Link-State Routing (OSPF) uses Dijkstra's algorithm with complete topology knowledge, while Distance Vector (RIP) uses the Bellman-Ford algorithm based on neighbor exchanges.
typesAndClassifications: Routing: Interior Gateway Protocols (OSPF, RIP) vs Exterior Gateway Protocols (BGP)
importantConcepts: Calculating Subnet Mask, Network ID, Broadcast ID, Usable Host Range
Dijkstra shortest path algorithm in OSPF
practicalApplications: VPC subnet design in AWS and Google Cloud

codeExamples.title: SubnetCalculation.txt
codeExamples.code:
IP Address: 192.168.10.65 / 26
Subnet Mask: 255.255.255.192 (11111111.11111111.11111111.11000000)
Host bits = 32 - 26 = 6 bits
Subnet Block Size = 2^6 = 64

Subnets:
Subnet 0: 192.168.10.0 to 192.168.10.63
Subnet 1: 192.168.10.64 to 192.168.10.127 (Contains our IP!)

Network Address: 192.168.10.64
First Usable Host: 192.168.10.65
Last Usable Host: 192.168.10.126
Broadcast Address: 192.168.10.127
Total Usable Hosts = 2^6 - 2 = 62
codeExamples.explanation: Step-by-step CIDR /26 subnet calculation.

complexityAnalysis.timeComplexity: Routing table lookup: O(1) via Trie / TCAM hardware
complexityAnalysis.explanation: Longest prefix match using TCAM.

commonMistakes: Forgetting to subtract 2 (for Network Address and Broadcast Address) when calculating usable hosts

interviewQuestions.question: How does a router perform Longest Prefix Match during packet forwarding?
interviewQuestions.answer: When a router receives a packet, it compares the destination IP address against its routing table. If multiple routes match, the router selects the entry with the longest prefix (most specific subnet mask), as it represents the most precise path to the destination.
interviewQuestions.tips: Explain why /28 is chosen over /24.

examQuestions.question: Given IP 172.16.0.0/16, divide it into 4 subnets using VLSM. Determine the subnet mask, network address, and usable range for each.

revisionNotes: CIDR /n: n network bits, 32-n host bits
Usable hosts = 2^(32-n) - 2
First address is Network ID; Last address is Broadcast ID

topics.title: Transport Layer: TCP, UDP, and Congestion Control
topics.summary: TCP 3-Way Handshake, 4-Way Teardown, UDP, Flow Control (Sliding Window), Congestion Control (Slow Start, Congestion Avoidance, Fast Retransmit, Fast Recovery).
topics.definition: The Transport Layer provides host-to-host process communication services, offering connection-oriented reliable transmission (TCP) or connectionless lightweight transmission (UDP).
topics.detailedExplanation: TCP provides reliable, ordered, error-checked, flow-controlled byte streams. Connection establishment uses the 3-Way Handshake (SYN -> SYN-ACK -> ACK), and connection termination uses a 4-Way Teardown (FIN -> ACK -> FIN -> ACK). Flow Control uses the Sliding Window protocol where receiver advertises its available buffer space (rwnd). Congestion Control protects the intermediate network using congestion window (cwnd): 1. Slow Start (exponential growth: cwnd doubles every RTT until ssthresh), 2. Congestion Avoidance (linear additive increase: cwnd increases by 1 MSS per RTT), 3. Fast Retransmit (3 duplicate ACKs trigger retransmission without waiting for timeout), and 4. Fast Recovery (multiplicative decrease). UDP provides connectionless, low-overhead datagrams with no ordering, retries, or flow control (ideal for DNS, VoIP, real-time gaming).
typesAndClassifications: TCP Congestion Control Algorithms (Tahoe, Reno, CUBIC, BBR)
importantConcepts: Sliding Window and flow control (rwnd vs cwnd)
Congestion control phases: Slow Start, Congestion Avoidance, Fast Retransmit, Fast Recovery

codeExamples.title: TcpHandshake.txt
codeExamples.code:
Client                                 Server
  |                                      |
  | -------- SYN (seq=x) --------------> | (Server listens on port)
  |                                      |
  | <------- SYN-ACK (seq=y, ack=x+1) -- | (Server acknowledges x)
  |                                      |
  | -------- ACK (seq=x+1, ack=y+1) ---> | (Connection ESTABLISHED)
  |                                      |
codeExamples.explanation: Diagrams the TCP 3-Way Handshake establishing synchronized sequence numbers.

complexityAnalysis.timeComplexity: Connection setup: 1 RTT; Data transmission: pipelined window
complexityAnalysis.explanation: Sliding window optimizes bandwidth-delay product.

commonMistakes: Confusing Flow Control (protects the receiver's buffer) with Congestion Control (protects the network routers and links from saturation)

interviewQuestions.question: Explain how TCP Congestion Control handles packet loss via 3 duplicate ACKs vs Timeout.
interviewQuestions.answer: 3 duplicate ACKs indicate mild network congestion (packets are still reaching receiver, but one was lost); TCP enters Fast Retransmit (retransmits missing packet immediately) and Fast Recovery (halves ssthresh and cwnd, avoiding slow start). A Timeout indicates severe congestion; TCP resets cwnd to 1 MSS and restarts with Slow Start.
interviewQuestions.tips: Contrast mild congestion (Fast Recovery) with severe congestion (Timeout reset to 1 MSS).

examQuestions.question: Describe the TCP 3-way handshake and 4-way termination with sequence diagrams.
examQuestions.solutionGuide: Draw ladder diagram for SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK and FIN, ACK, FIN, ACK; explain TIME_WAIT state.

practiceExercises: Calculate maximum throughput of a TCP connection given RTT = 50ms and Window Size = 64KB.
revisionNotes: TCP 3-way handshake: SYN -> SYN-ACK -> ACK
Flow control uses rwnd (receiver buffer); Congestion control uses cwnd
UDP is fast and connectionless; TCP is reliable and ordered

topics.title: Application Layer Protocols and Network Security
topics.summary: DNS resolution, HTTP/1.1 vs HTTP/2 vs HTTP/3, TLS/SSL handshake, asymmetric vs symmetric encryption, and firewalls.
topics.definition: Application Layer protocols define the rules for end-user network communication, while Network Security safeguards transmitted data through cryptographic protocols.
topics.detailedExplanation: DNS (Domain Name System) translates human-readable hostnames to IP addresses through recursive resolvers, root servers, TLD servers, and authoritative nameservers. HTTP evolution: HTTP/1.1 introduced persistent keep-alive connections but suffered from Head-of-Line (HoL) blocking; HTTP/2 introduced binary framing, multiplexing multiple streams over a single TCP connection, and server push; HTTP/3 replaces TCP with QUIC (UDP-based) to eliminate transport-layer HoL blocking and 0-RTT handshakes. HTTPS encrypts HTTP traffic via TLS (Transport Layer Security). The TLS Handshake uses Asymmetric Encryption (RSA or ECDHE) to authenticate the server and securely agree on a shared Session Key, after which high-speed Symmetric Encryption (AES-GCM) encrypts payload data.
typesAndClassifications: Application Protocols (HTTP, DNS, SMTP, FTP, SSH)
importantConcepts: HTTP/2 multiplexing vs HTTP/3 QUIC over UDP
Public key cryptography vs Symmetric encryption
practicalApplications: Deploying SSL/TLS certificates with Let's Encrypt

codeExamples.title: TlsHandshake.txt
codeExamples.code:
Client                                 Server
  |                                      |
  | --- ClientHello (TLS ver, cipher) -> |
  |                                      |
  | <-- ServerHello, Certificate, Key -- | (Server sends X.509 cert + ECDHE param)
  |                                      |
  | (Client verifies CA signature)       |
  | --- ClientKeyExchange (ECDHE param)- | (Both derive identical shared Symmetric Key)
  |                                      |
  | <=== Encrypted Application Data ===> | (High-speed AES-GCM symmetric encryption)
codeExamples.explanation: Asymmetric exchange generates symmetric session key.

complexityAnalysis.timeComplexity: TLS handshake: 1 RTT (TLS 1.3) or 0-RTT (session resumption)
complexityAnalysis.explanation: TLS 1.3 combines key exchange into first flight.

commonMistakes: Believing asymmetric encryption encrypts entire web session payloads (it only negotiates the symmetric session key)

interviewQuestions.question: What happens from a networking perspective when you type https://www.google.com into your browser and press Enter?
interviewQuestions.answer: 1. Browser checks local DNS cache; if missing, recursive resolver queries Root -> TLD (.com) -> Authoritative DNS. 2. Browser receives IP address and initiates TCP 3-way handshake on port 443. 3. TLS handshake executes: certificate validated, symmetric session key derived. 4. Browser sends HTTP GET request over encrypted tunnel. 5. Server responds with HTML payload; browser parses, fetches assets, and renders page.
interviewQuestions.tips: Walk chronologically through DNS -> TCP -> TLS -> HTTP -> DOM render.

examQuestions.question: Explain how DNS resolution works with a diagram showing root, TLD, and authoritative servers.
examQuestions.solutionGuide: Show iterative vs recursive queries, root servers (.), TLD (.com), and domain nameserver.

practiceExercises: Inspect the TLS certificate of a website using openssl s_client -connect google.com:443.
revisionNotes: DNS resolves names to IPs over UDP port 53
HTTP/2 multiplexes over 1 TCP connection; HTTP/3 uses QUIC over UDP
TLS uses asymmetric keys to negotiate symmetric AES session key

topics.title: HTML, Modern CSS, and Responsive Design
topics.summary: Semantic HTML5, CSS Box Model, Flexbox, Grid, CSS Variables, Media Queries, and Tailwind utility-first styling.
topics.definition: HTML structures content on the web semantically, while CSS describes the visual presentation, layout, and responsiveness across varied device screens.
topics.detailedExplanation: Semantic HTML5 (<header>, <main>, <nav>, <article>, <section>, <footer>) enhances accessibility (ARIA) and search engine indexing. The CSS Box Model comprises Content, Padding, Border, and Margin (box-sizing: border-box ensures padding and borders are included within specified dimensions). Flexbox provides one-dimensional layout control (axes, alignment, distribution), while CSS Grid provides two-dimensional layout control (rows and columns). Responsive design employs fluid layouts, responsive typography (rem, ch), and media queries (min-width mobile-first). Utility-first frameworks like Tailwind CSS eliminate separate CSS files by applying atomic styling classes directly to markup.
importantConcepts: CSS Grid grid-template-columns, fr units, gap
practicalApplications: Accessible web applications adhering to WCAG 2.1 AA standards
Modern responsive SaaS landing pages and dashboards

codeExamples.explanation: Fluid CSS Grid with auto-fit and minmax adapting to any viewport width.

complexityAnalysis.timeComplexity: CSSOM tree construction and layout calculation: browser sub-millisecond
complexityAnalysis.explanation: Browser rendering pipeline: DOM -> CSSOM -> Render Tree -> Layout -> Paint.

commonMistakes: Omitting <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1.0"> in HTML header

interviewQuestions.question: Explain the CSS Box Model and how box-sizing: border-box changes it.
interviewQuestions.answer: The CSS box model consists of content, padding, border, and margin. In the default content-box model, width and height only apply to the content; adding padding and border expands the total element size. With box-sizing: border-box, padding and border are included within the specified width and height, preventing layout breakage.
interviewQuestions.tips: Contrast content-box vs border-box formulas.

examQuestions.question: Compare Flexbox and CSS Grid layouts. When should each be utilized?
examQuestions.solutionGuide: Flexbox is 1D (rows OR columns); Grid is 2D (rows AND columns simultaneously); give layout examples.
